Official inquiries and expert reports provide clear, actionable steps to prevent preventable deaths among vulnerable unhoused populations.

Bureaucratic inertia and delayed sign-offs leave crucial safety protocols unimplemented while fatalities remain persistently high.

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: Recommendations to reduce deaths of homeless people, and support bereaved families, yet to be acted on years later ===

[Source 1 — www.dublininquirer.com] (URL: https://www.dublininquirer.com/recommendations-to-reduce-deaths-of-homeless-people-and-support-bereaved-families-yet-to-be-acted-on-years-later/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Recommendations to reduce deaths of homeless people, and support bereaved families, yet to be acted on years later

At least 46 people died last year while homeless in Dublin.

Actual Article Body:
It depends, in part, on whether the owners can prove they've been holiday lets for more than seven years – and whether planning enforcement noticed.

The tender document for the design says the framework has a maximum estimated value of €7.5 million. It also gives a tentative construction estimate of €25 million.

Social tenants, including children, are often locked out of communal areas in their complexes. Would it help if they were represented at the OMCs' meetings?

At least 46 people died last year while homeless in Dublin.

At least 46 people died while homeless in Dublin last year, according to the Dublin Region Homeless Executive (DRHE).

That's pretty similar to the number of people who died while homeless in 2020. Even while the number of people who are homeless nearly doubled in those years.

In December 2020, there were 6,022 people who were homeless in Dublin, according to government figures. By December 2025, that figure was 11,782.

But the number of deaths could be lower, if the recommendations of a 2020 report from Dr Austin O’Carroll, an inner-city GP and founder of Safetynet, which provides healthcare to homeless people, had been implemented, says Sinn Féin TD Eoin Ó Broin.

“People are not getting the supports they need for addiction and mental health,” Ó Broin says. “We’re not doing anything differently from what we were doing a few years ago.”

The Housing First programme, which is supposed to provide those supports and lift people out of homelessness too, has stalled, says Ó Broin.

One of the recommendations of O'Carroll's report was to bring in a system for reviewing the deaths of people in homelessness.

Work on setting up that review system to gather learning from homeless deaths and issue recommendations is nearing completion, Dr O’Carroll said by phone on Monday.

Likewise, the DRHE still has not brought in a protocol for homeless services on what to do when someone dies in a hostel. That's something independent Councillor Mannix Flynn asked for in 2023, following the death of a relative.

A spokesperson for DRHE said that it is waiting on sign-off from the HSE and hopes to publish that protocol in the coming weeks.

DRHE figures for 2025 show that 27 people who were living in hostels run by private companies passed away, as well as 16 people living in charity-run hostels, and three others who were known to the outreach team, meaning they were homeless and had a history of sleeping rough.

In 2020, a similar number of people died in homeless services, according to Dr O’Carroll’s 2021 report: 48 homeless people died while living in emergency accommodation or rough sleeping.

Counting can get complicated, because definitions of who is homeless, and who is included in these numbers can vary.

The 48 people who died in 2020 don't include an additional 21 people who died while living in long-term accommodation, funded by homeless services.

Likewise, the 46 who died in 2025 don't include people who died while living in long-term accommodation, funded by homeless services. It's unclear how many people that might have been.

"The DRHE does not report on deaths occurring in Long-Term Accommodation (LTA) or any other housing, as individuals residing in LTA are not considered to be homeless,” a DRHE spokesperson said.

The Health Research Board (HRB) also doesn’t count those in long-term accommodation run by homeless charities – but does include others living in very insecure or very substandard accommodation.

While the death rate appears to be dropping, because the homeless population has increased significantly, Ó Broin says he understands that the cohort of homeless people with very complex needs has not increased significantly.

A spokesperson for the DRHE didn’t comment on the causes of death.

"The Department of Health commissioned the HRB to collect data on all deaths which occur among people who are homeless nationally,” she said. “To address the need to improve understanding of premature mortality and to provide more complete and accurate national data to inform policy.”

In a report published this year, the Health Research Board examined the causes of death for 124 people (81 percent male) who died while homeless nationally in 2022.

Over a third of deaths (36 percent) were due to poisoning, meaning drug overdose. Methadone was the most common specific drug implicated in poisoning deaths.

The other deaths were classified as medical (most commonly, cardiovascular conditions), or traumatic (most commonly, falls).

“Many people take their own lives in homeless services,” says Flynn. He asked the council in 2023 to increase training for staff to intervene in those cases.

The number of deaths among homeless people in Dublin increased during the Covid-19 lockdown period but most were not caused by the virus directly, according to Dr O'Carroll, who told Newstalk he thought there were three or four Covid-19 deaths among that cohort in 2020 and 2021.

Anti-homelessness campaigner Father Peter McVerry said in late 2020 that many of the support services homeless people rely on, like day centres, which normally provide people with a social outlet were closed during the lockdowns.

Residential drug treatment centres closed. Some day services for drug users were also not meeting people face-to-face, he said. “Isolation leads to a lot of depression and that has been widely reported,” he said.

That increase in the death rate during the lockdown prompted calls for the adult safeguarding reviews, a process in place in the UK to gather learnings from the deaths, which could improve services.

Speaking this week, Dr O’Carroll said he is waiting on sign-off for legal documentation to set up the new review system, for which he will be the clinical lead.

“I gave the documents to the legal experts, and they took a year or two to sort out,” he says. “It is supposed to come back to me in the next few weeks.”

In the meantime, he has worked with the HSE to provide feedback to some homeless services on a small number of individual cases.

“Once the process is in place, we can stand over the findings legally, and therefore I can start issuing recommendations on an annual basis,” says O’Carroll.

In his 2021 report one of his other recommendations was setting up evidence-based initiatives to reduce the risk of death by overdose, such as making naloxone – a drug which can bring people out of an opiate overdose – available in all homeless services.

He also called for initiatives to reduce long-term homelessness, improve primary care in privately run hostels, and increase mental-health supports, especially for people who have both mental-health difficulties and addictions.

Naloxone is now available in hostels, O'Carroll says.

However the other types of supports remain patchy.

The Review of the Homeless Action Plan 2022 to 2024 found that “wraparound supports are inconsistent or unavailable”, it says.

“Nearly every group flagged concerns about private emergency accommodation (PEA): the cost of, the standard and need for trauma-informed model of care,” says the report.

And that remains an issue, according to a DRHE report issued last year

Ó Broin, the Sinn Féin TD, says deaths in homelessness remain high because most of Dr O’Carroll’s recommendations have not been implemented.

There needs to be a renewed focus on those people in homeless services with high support needs, mental health difficulties, trauma, and addiction.

Because of the focus on homeless families, “the specific needs of those with very complex needs are even more marginalised”, he says.

Similarly, Flynn, the independent councillor, says that “There is a serious gap when it comes to the most vulnerable."

There is stigma faced by families whose loved ones pass away in emergency accommodation, Flynn says.

He thinks the council needs a process in place to include families and friends and to remember the person who died, he says.

He would like to see memorials within hostels to acknowledge those who died, he says. “When it comes to having a simple, dignified ritual,” he says.

Laoise Neylon is a reporter at Dublin Inquirer. You can reach her at lneylon@dublininquirer.com.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Will Seattle's proposed RV rules help people living in them? Critics have doubts

Seattle City Councilmember Dan Strauss is leading the charge on a proposal that he hopes will get RVs off residential streets and connect people to housing. Some people have reservations about whether this plan will actually benefit people who live in these vehicles.

Actual Article Body:
Seattle could see fewer RVs on its streets next summer if the City Council votes to change parking rules for these vehicles.

The proposed change would ban RV parking on city streets for more than two hours and require people living in RVs to get permits to park their vehicles in industrial areas. Additionally, service providers will offer shelter to individuals living in RVs and, if a person refuses after six “appropriate” offers, they’ll lose the permit.

City Councilmember Dan Strauss is leading the charge on this proposed change for RVs, which he said are too big to be on city streets. Strauss represents Seattle’s District 6, which includes Ballard, Magnolia, and Phinney Ridge. The City Council could vote on these changes as early as Oct. 20.

“ We've got all of these different types of services that are built for specific populations of folks that are experiencing homelessness,” Strauss said in an interview with KUOW’s “Soundside.” “We do not have any of those services set up for people who live in their vehicles.”

But some people, like Alison Eisinger, are skeptical that this change will actually help people who live in RVs.

Eisinger, who serves as the executive director for the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, agreed with some of the proposed changes, like establishing safe parking lots for RVs and implementing skilled outreach to people living in these vehicles.

However, she had concerns about the proposal overall. She said it’s too complicated and expensive.

“We're not talking about people who are living in their vacation homes. We're not talking about a van life person,” Eisinger said. “We're talking about people who are too poor to have another place to live, and I really think we should be able to make better policy and spend our limited homelessness services dollars in better ways than what's currently on the table here.”

The proposal would draw on a mix of $1.5 million in one-time funding and $3.5 million in ongoing funding. Strauss, who chairs the City Council’s Budget Committee, said implementing these changes will cost more in the first year and require fewer dollars over time to maintain, especially because the permitting program would be temporary.

Like Eisinger, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson expressed reservations about the complexity and cost of the changes, which she discussed during a live call-in segment with “Soundside” in early October.

“ If we do this poorly, what can happen is that we are possessing people's RVs and putting more people into unsheltered homelessness or just chasing them away to another neighborhood or city,” Wilson said.

Strauss acknowledged these concerns and said that’s why he set aside a longer lead time to get these changes rolling. If passed, the proposal would go into effect on April 30, and enforcement would start in the summer.

“Running government is a complex task, and we cannot look away from addressing these vehicles on our streets right now,” Strauss said. “And to say that it is too complex to address means that we are not serving Seattleites.”

Neal Lampi is no longer a Seattleite, but a few years ago this change would have impacted him. Lampi, who’s now in Lake Forest Park, lived in an RV around Seattle for seven years.

He was sympathetic to peoples’ frustrations, acknowledging he wouldn’t want to see an RV parked in front of his home or place of work.

But Lampi pointed out that people living in these vehicles are dealing with a lot, too.

“There’s a lot of hostility out on the street, and I’m not talking about between homeless people,” he said. “I’m talking about [hostility] against homeless people.”

The post Statins May Protect People From Glaucoma or Blindness By Preventing or Slowing Nerve Cell Death appeared first on Good News Network.

Actual Article Body:
Statins may be protecting people from more than just cholesterol, suggests new research from the University of California in San Diego.

Patients with glaucoma who take the cholesterol-busting pills appear less likely to need surgery—and have a reduced chance of the condition worsening, according to the findings.

Called the “silent thief of sight” because the vision loss usually occurs slowly over a long period of time, glaucoma may cause blindness if left untreated, damaging the optic nerve, which transmits visual information from the eye to the brain.

The new study, published online in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, found that people who already have glaucoma who are taking statins appear less likely to need stronger treatments, such as extra eye drops or surgery to keep it under control.

“Statins are prescribed to lower cholesterol levels but studies have indicated that they may also prevent or slow nerve cell death,” said study author Dr. Robert Weinreb.

But their potential role in preventing or slowing down glaucoma—a leading cause of irreversible blindness which permanently damages the optic nerve—is poorly understood.

Dr. Weinreb and his team searched a large global database covering 165 million people and compared more than 210,000 patients who had a record of statin use between 2006 and 2026 with a matched control group of 210,000 people who had no record of using statins. People in both groups had to have a recorded ophthalmological follow up.

The findings show that statins were linked to a lower risk of the individual progressing to need glaucoma surgery—or any other treatment.

• Statin use was associated with a 15% lower risk of developing the most common form of the progressive eye disease.

• At five years, statin use was associated with a 36% lower risk of incisional glaucoma surgery and a 55% reduced risk of minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), a keyhole procedure to lower the intraocular pressure in the eye.

• Statins were also associated with a 60% lower risk of ‘selective laser trabeculoplasty’ (SLT), a procedure that lowers the pressure in the eye by using laser pulses.

• There was also a 12% reduced risk of (needing) eye drops to reduce the pressure in the eye—linked to statin use.”

And after 10 years, statin use continued to be associated with a lower risk of incision glaucoma surgery, MIGS, SLT, and use of eye drops.

RELATED: Dyson Award Goes to First Ever Device to Monitor Glaucoma Symptoms From Home

In a separate analysis, more than 30,000 people with glaucoma who were taking statins were compared with almost 250,000 with glaucoma who weren’t taking the drug.

Although these were observational studies, so no firm conclusions can be drawn about cause and effect, the findings add to the growing literature about the neuro-protective effect of statin drugs.

“Running government is a complex task, and we cannot look away from addressing these vehicles on our streets right now,” Strauss said. “And to say that it is too complex to address means that we are not serving Seattleites.”

Neal Lampi is no longer a Seattleite, but a few years ago this change would have impacted him. Lampi, who’s now in Lake Forest Park, lived in an RV around Seattle for seven years.

He was sympathetic to peoples’ frustrations, acknowledging he wouldn’t want to see an RV parked in front of his home or place of work.

But Lampi pointed out that people living in these vehicles are dealing with a lot, too.

“There’s a lot of hostility out on the street, and I’m not talking about between homeless people,” he said. “I’m talking about [hostility] against homeless people.”

Actual Article Body:
Statins may be protecting people from more than just cholesterol, suggests new research from the University of California in San Diego.

Patients with glaucoma who take the cholesterol-busting pills appear less likely to need surgery—and have a reduced chance of the condition worsening, according to the findings.

Called the “silent thief of sight” because the vision loss usually occurs slowly over a long period of time, glaucoma may cause blindness if left untreated, damaging the optic nerve, which transmits visual information from the eye to the brain.

The new study, published online in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, found that people who already have glaucoma who are taking statins appear less likely to need stronger treatments, such as extra eye drops or surgery to keep it under control.

“Statins are prescribed to lower cholesterol levels but studies have indicated that they may also prevent or slow nerve cell death,” said study author Dr. Robert Weinreb.

But their potential role in preventing or slowing down glaucoma—a leading cause of irreversible blindness which permanently damages the optic nerve—is poorly understood.

Dr. Weinreb and his team searched a large global database covering 165 million people and compared more than 210,000 patients who had a record of statin use between 2006 and 2026 with a matched control group of 210,000 people who had no record of using statins. People in both groups had to have a recorded ophthalmological follow up.

The findings show that statins were linked to a lower risk of the individual progressing to need glaucoma surgery—or any other treatment.

• Statin use was associated with a 15% lower risk of developing the most common form of the progressive eye disease.

• At five years, statin use was associated with a 36% lower risk of incisional glaucoma surgery and a 55% reduced risk of minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS), a keyhole procedure to lower the intraocular pressure in the eye.

• Statins were also associated with a 60% lower risk of ‘selective laser trabeculoplasty’ (SLT), a procedure that lowers the pressure in the eye by using laser pulses.

• There was also a 12% reduced risk of (needing) eye drops to reduce the pressure in the eye—linked to statin use.”

And after 10 years, statin use continued to be associated with a lower risk of incision glaucoma surgery, MIGS, SLT, and use of eye drops.

In a separate analysis, more than 30,000 people with glaucoma who were taking statins were compared with almost 250,000 with glaucoma who weren’t taking the drug.

Although these were observational studies, so no firm conclusions can be drawn about cause and effect, the findings add to the growing literature about the neuro-protective effect of statin drugs.
